newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Data shows Australian budget on track - analysis.
newsitem.headline: Data shows Australian budget on track - analysis.

text.p: Analysis of Australian government financial statistics suggests that Canberra is broadly on track to meet the fiscal forecasts issued in the Mid-Year Review in January.

An examination of the progress shown so far this year by revenue and expenditure suggests a final figure not far from the A$8.5 billion 1996/97 underlying deficit that the government projected in January.
The Reuters analysis, checked with fiscal analysts who asked not to be identified, avoids seasonal effects by assessing the budget on a rolling 12-month basis.
On such a basis, the budget has already bettered the projection. For the 12 months to February, the underlying deficit was only A$8.2 billion.

The situation is flattered, however, by an extra lump of company tax collected in November -- the last of a series of bring-forwards that former prime minister Paul Keating announced five years ago, requiring companies to pay their tax earlier.
So revenue cannot be expected to maintain the same trajectory in the final four months of the fiscal year.
REVENUE
Revenue for the 12 months to June last year was A$121.6 billion. The Mid-Year Review projected A$128.8 billion for the 12 months to June 1997.

If revenue rose in a straight line from June 1996 to June 1997, then by the end of February it would have covered two-thirds of the gap between those two figures -- that is, it would have reached A$126.3 billion.
In fact, 12-month revenue in February was A$127.0 billion, suggesting the budget is ahead of schedule.
The picture is distorted, however, by the extra company tax, which was collected in November, and by the December settlement of a tax dispute over oil resource tax in Victoria.

Both of those factors have injected lumps of money into the budget that will not recur in the final four months of the year, and an estimate of the final June 12-month revenue figure requires allowance for their effect.

Assuming revenue maintains the same progress it has shown so far this year, but allowing for the two big distortions, then the final 12-month revenue figure in June would be around A$128 billion, which is less than currently projected.
EXPENDITURE
However, expenditure is ahead of schedule so far and the effect of the Victorian tax settlement suggests that it should be even better by the end of the year.
The government spent A$132.0 billion in 1996 (in underlying terms) and in January it projected 12-month spending for June 1997 at A$137.3 billion.
To reach this target in a straight line, the underlying 12-month spending for February would be A$135.5 billion.
In fact it was a little lower, at A$135.3 billion.

But this better-than-expected performance has been achieved despite a large one-off lump of spending in December. Since this lump will not happen again in the final four months of the year, spending seems to be heading further below projections.

The lump is the other side of the Victorian resource tax settlement. A dispute over tax liability was finally settled with a set of circular payments in which the federal government both gave and received about A$600 million.

Assuming expenditure maintains the same progress it has shown so far this year, but allowing for the distortion, then the final 12-month expenditure figure in June would be between A$136.5 billion and A$137.0 billion.
BROADLY ON TRACK

According to this analysis, the government's finances are heading for a 12-month underlying deficit in June between A$8.5 billion and A$9 billion, quite close to the projected figure of A$8.5 billion.
However, government finances are highly volatile and the analysis gives an imprecise picture of what is happening.
Moreover, a close examination of budget detail raises many unanswered questions about the flow of revenue and expenditure under particular headings.
To cite just one of the larger confusing details, the current trajectory of defence spending will undershoot the department's full-year target by A$460 million.
Since the defence budget is only around A$10 billion, this hardly seems likely.
